description: Mission team for the space mission game design and development
summary: Git Push To Mars_Mission Studio is an interactive Python and Pygame space mission design simulator and four-player cooperative Mission Control game developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We built a two-phase desktop application that combines a 4 tab Systems Engineering Studio with a real-time Runge-Kutta (RK4) multi-body Orbital Flight Engine. Our solution addresses the challenge by modeling the six coupled resources that govern real spaceflight: Mass, Power, Budget, Data Generation, Communications Capacity, and Time/Delta-V. Using authentic NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) instrument profiles, JPL Horizons orbital parameters, and Deep Space Network (DSN) downlink specifications, players select launch vehicles, size solar arrays for Mars's 43% solar flux, and balance Tsiolkovsky propellant margins. Up to four teammates divide roles across Flight Dynamics (FDO), Spacecraft Bus (BUS), Science (SCI), and Communications (COM) consoles to approve designs, execute Trans-Mars Injection burns, and resolve mid-flight Solar Flare emergencies together. This project is important because professional astrodynamics tools like NASA GMAT have steep learning curves, while commercial space games ignore coupled subsystem constraints. By turning complex mathematical trade-offs into visual, collaborative gameplay—and exporting executable GMAT .script files—our studio bridges classroom STEM learning and real-world aerospace engineering for students and citizen scientists everywhere.
details:
Git Push To Mars_Mission Studio (gitpushtomars_missionstudio.py) is an interactive space mission design simulator and four-player cooperative Mission Control application built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.

What It Does & How It Works

The application operates as a two-phase aerospace engineering and flight simulation platform that guides players from initial blueprint assembly to interplanetary orbital operations:

  • Phase 1 (4-Tab Engineering Studio): Players select mission objectives (Earth Climate, Lunar Scout, Mars Explorer, or Sandbox), target orbits, launch vehicles, spacecraft buses, DSN antennas, and up to three NASA PDS payloads.
  • Real-Time 6-Resource Gate: As components are toggled, an integrated physics dashboard calculates wet mass, solar power balance, total budget, daily data generation, DSN downlink capacity, and Tsiolkovsky delta-V margins.
  • Phase 2 (Live Orbital Flight): Upon launch, a fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) multi-body propagator simulates heliocentric trajectories across the gravitational fields of the Sun, Earth, Moon, and Mars.
  • 4-Station Mission Control: Players coordinate across four consoles—Flight Dynamics (FDO), Spacecraft Bus (BUS), Science (SCI), and Communications (COM)—to fire Trans-Mars Injection burns and resolve Solar Flare alerts.
  • Debrief & GMAT Export: Completed missions generate a graded engineering scorecard (/ 1000 points) and export a valid NASA General Mission Analysis Tool (.script) file for external astrodynamics verification.

Key Benefits

  • Visualizing Coupled Trade-Offs: Players immediately see how mounting a heavy radar payload increases dry mass, reduces orbital delta-V, drains eclipse battery reserves, and challenges Deep Space Network downlink bandwidth.
  • Accessible Astrodynamics: Complex orbital mechanics—including inverse-square solar flux drop-off at Mars, Hohmann transfer phasing, and solid-state recorder buffer management—are translated into intuitive visual feedback.
  • Collaborative Decision-Making: By splitting responsibilities across four distinct Mission Control stations, teams practice real-world systems engineering negotiation under strict mass, power, and funding caps.

Intended Impact

  • Bridging STEM Education and Industry Tooling: Professional suites like NASA GMAT have steep learning curves, whereas commercial games rarely enforce coupled subsystem constraints; our studio bridges both worlds.
  • Empowering Citizen Scientists: Students and educators can test real mission architectures in minutes and export their designs directly into executable NASA GMAT scripts for classroom or research analysis.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Programming Language & Engine: Developed in Python 3.12 using Pygame 2.x (SDL2) for real-time 2D vector rendering, orbital trail plotting, and event-driven UI state management.
  • Physics & Math Libraries: Built with Python's native math, json, and socket modules to compute RK4 gravitational integration, Tsiolkovsky rocket equations, and local leaderboard persistence.
  • Development Environment & Hardware: Engineered in Visual Studio Code with Git/GitLens version control and tested on Apple Silicon macOS hardware with Retina HiDPI coordinate normalization.
  • NASA Open Data & References: Parameterized using NASA GMAT Keplerian state standards, NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris constants, NASA PDS instrument profiles, and NASA DSN dish specifications.

How the Project Is Creative

  • Asymmetric 4-Player Co-Op Loop: Instead of a single-player sandbox, we turned spacecraft design into a live Mission Control role-playing experience where FDO, BUS, SCI, and COM must sign off on hardware changes and jointly survive mid-flight crises.
  • Game-to-GMAT Pipeline: Integrating a one-click .script code generator inside a Pygame interface turns a playable hackathon game into a functional pre-phase-A mission design utility.
  • Deterministic Demo Triggers: We built live hotkeys ([T] for GMAT Mars Transfer Burn, [F9] for Solar Flare Radiation Surge, and [TAB] for studio switching) so teams and judges can test critical mission phases on demand.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Realism vs. Playability: We scaled multi-year interplanetary transits into a 2-to-5-minute interactive loop using configurable time-warp (1x to 10x) while preserving authentic mass, power, and delta-V ratios.
  • Cross-Platform UI Reliability: To prevent macOS Dock clipping and Retina display mouse-scaling offsets, we engineered a locked 1100x640 viewport with dynamic window-to-surface coordinate normalization and full keyboard navigation.
  • Educational Transparency: Every orbital regime, rocket, and PDS sensor includes inline engineering notes explaining why a mission succeeded or failed during the post-flight debrief.
